content: Norelgestromin and Ethinyl Estradiol is a combination hormonal contraceptive (CHC) approved by the FDA for pregnancy prevention in women who choose to use a transdermal patch. It is important to note that this medication carries a Black Box Warning, which highlights significant risks associated with its use. Common Adverse Reactions The most frequently reported side effects include breast symptoms, nausea, vomiting, headaches, application site reactions, abdominal pain, dysmenorrhea, vaginal bleeding, menstrual disorders, and mood or anxiety disturbances. Indications and Dosage for Adults Norelgestromin/Ethinyl Estradiol is indicated for contraception in women who prefer a transdermal patch. However, its effectiveness may be reduced in women weighing 198 lbs (90 kg) or more. How to Use the Patch The patch follows a 28-day cycle. A new patch is applied weekly for three weeks (21 days total), followed by a patch-free week during which withdrawal bleeding is expected. Each new patch should be applied on the same day of the week, known as the Patch Change Day. Only one patch should be worn at a time, and it should not be cut, damaged, or altered, as this may compromise contraceptive efficacy. After the patch-free week, a new cycle begins with a new patch. There should never be more than a seven-day patch-free interval between cycles. Starting the Patch Women can start the patch in one of two ways: 1. Apply the first patch within the first 24 hours of menstruation. 2. Apply the first patch on the first Sunday after menstruation begins. In this case, a non-hormonal backup contraceptive (e.g., condoms with spermicide) is required for the first seven days of the initial cycle. If switching from oral contraceptives or a vaginal ring, the first patch should be applied on the day the next pill or ring would have been started. If menstruation does not occur within a week after the last active pill or ring removal, pregnancy should be ruled out before starting the patch. Postpartum and Post-Abortion Use Postpartum: Start no earlier than four weeks after childbirth in non-breastfeeding women due to an increased risk of thromboembolism. If menstruation has not resumed, consider the possibility of ovulation and conception before starting the patch. Use a backup contraceptive for the first seven days. After a first-trimester abortion or miscarriage: The patch can be started immediately without the need for additional contraception. If not started within five days, follow the instructions for first-time users and use a backup method. Application Instructions The patch can be placed on the upper outer arm, abdomen, buttock, or back, avoiding areas where tight clothing may rub. It should not be applied to the breasts, irritated skin, or the same location as the previous patch. The skin should be clean and dry, free of lotions, creams, oils, powders, or makeup. Press the patch firmly for 10 seconds to ensure full adhesion and check daily to confirm it remains secure. If the Patch Becomes Loose or Falls Off If detached for less than one day, reapply it or use a new patch immediately. No backup contraception is needed, and the Patch Change Day remains the same. If detached for more than one day or if unsure, apply a new patch and start a new four-week cycle. Use backup contraception for the first week of the new cycle. Missed Patch Changes At the start of a cycle (Week 1/Day 1): Apply a new patch as soon as remembered. Use backup contraception for the first week. Mid-cycle (Week 2/Day 8 or Week 3/Day 15): If delayed by one or two days, apply a new patch immediately and continue the cycle as usual. No backup contraception is needed. If delayed by more than two days, start a new cycle and use backup contraception for one week. End of cycle (Week 4/Day 22): If the patch is not removed on time, remove it as soon as remembered and start the next cycle on the usual Patch Change Day. Changing the Patch Change Day Complete the current cycle, remove the third patch on the correct day, and during the patch-free week, apply a new patch on the desired day. Ensure no more than seven consecutive patch-free days. Contraindications Do not prescribe Norelgestromin/Ethinyl Estradiol to women with: High risk of arterial or venous thrombotic diseases (e.g., smokers over 35, history of deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, cerebrovascular disease, coronary artery disease, or thrombogenic heart conditions). Uncontrolled hypertension or diabetes with vascular disease. Migraines with aura or focal neurological symptoms. Liver tumors or severe liver disease. Breast cancer or other estrogen/progestin-sensitive cancers. Undiagnosed abnormal uterine bleeding. Pregnancy. Warnings Thromboembolic Disorders: Discontinue use if a thrombotic event occurs or if there is unexplained vision loss, proptosis, diplopia, papilledema, or retinal vascular lesions. Evaluate for retinal vein thrombosis immediately. Surgery and Immobilization: Stop the patch at least four weeks before and two weeks after major surgery or prolonged immobilization. Postpartum Use: Start no earlier than four weeks after delivery in non-breastfeeding women due to increased VTE risk. Liver Disease: Discontinue use if jaundice or liver dysfunction occurs. Hypertension: Monitor blood pressure and discontinue use if it rises significantly. Gallbladder Disease: Use with caution in women with a history of gallbladder disease or pregnancy-related cholestasis. Carbohydrate and Lipid Effects: Monitor diabetic or prediabetic women closely. Consider alternative contraception for women with uncontrolled dyslipidemia. Adverse Effects and Monitoring Headaches: Evaluate new, recurrent, or severe headaches and discontinue use if indicated. Breakthrough Bleeding: Continue treatment if unscheduled bleeding occurs, but investigate persistent or recurrent abnormal bleeding to rule out pregnancy or malignancy. Pharmacokinetics The pharmacokinetic profile of Ethinyl Estradiol in the patch differs from oral contraceptives, with higher steady-state concentrations (Css) and lower peak concentrations (Cmax). This may increase estrogen exposure and the risk of adverse events, including venous thromboembolism. Pediatric Use The safety and efficacy of Norelgestromin/Ethinyl Estradiol have been established in post-pubertal adolescents under 18 years of age. It is not indicated for use before menarche. Off-Label Use There is limited information regarding off-label use in both adult and pediatric populations. This detailed guidance ensures the safe and effective use of Norelgestromin/Ethinyl Estradiol while minimizing risks associated with its use.
